pairs.rationale: John connects receiving Him and believing in His name with becoming children born of God. The letter celebrates being called children of God and being so; its additional world-not-knowing explanation is not inserted into the Gospel’s birth description.

Philippians anticipates the Savior transforming the lowly body to conform to His glorious body. The letter anticipates being like Him when He is manifested and seeing Him as He is. The hope of likeness preserves the different bodily and seeing formulations.

Paul urges cleansing ourselves from flesh-and-spirit defilement in light of promises and completing holiness in fear of God. The letter connects hope in Him with self-purification as He is pure. The grounds and comparison are related without making all descriptions identical.

Both define sin through morally negative conduct: here sin is lawlessness; later all unrighteousness is sin. The later distinction concerning sin not leading to death remains its additional statement, not a change to this definition.

Hebrews describes the high priest as tested in every way as we are, yet without sin. The letter says there is no sin in Him, alongside His manifestation to take away sins. The target supports sinlessness without printing the whole manifestation claim.

The earlier test calls claiming to know Him while not keeping His commandments a lie. This verse joins abiding with not sinning and says the sinner has neither seen nor known Him. The conduct-and-knowledge test preserves both verses’ unsoftened formulations without inserting an unstated frequency qualification.

Both connect the practice of righteousness with His righteousness. The earlier verse also connects that practitioner with having been born of Him; this verse warns against being led astray. The repeated criterion does not settle an unprinted pronoun antecedent.

Jesus describes the devil as a murderer from the beginning and a liar whose desires are followed by His opponents. The letter connects practicing sin with the devil sinning from the beginning and the Son undoing his works. The different charges and the letter’s additional purpose remain explicit.

Both state that the one born of God does not sin. Here abiding seed and inability to sin are the given explanations; later keeping himself and the evil one not touching him are stated. The actual keeps-himself wording is preserved and neither passage receives an imported habitual qualification.

The later call to love says the lover is born of God and knows God, while the nonlover has not known God. Here lack of righteousness or brother-love marks one not from God. The shared birth, belonging and love test preserves the distinct stated criteria.

Jesus commands love for one another as He loved the disciples. The letter names love for one another as the message heard from the beginning. The Gospel’s new-commandment description and the letter’s beginning description are retained without inventing a date for that beginning.

Genesis narrates Cain killing his brother Abel and God confronting him concerning his brother and the crying blood. The letter identifies Cain and explains his evil works against his brother’s righteous works. That explicit moral motive is not falsely quoted as part of the retained Genesis narrative.

Jesus tells disciples that the world hated Him before them and explains that it hates those He chose out of it. The letter tells brothers not to be surprised if the world hates them. The comparison preserves the different audiences and the Gospel’s stated prior hatred.

Both speak of having passed from death into life. Jesus connects this with hearing His word and believing the One who sent Him; the letter says love for the brothers is how we know it. The shared transition preserves the distinct stated evidence and conditions.

Jesus moves from the murder prohibition to anger against a brother and liability to judgment. The letter calls brother-hatred murder and excludes abiding eternal life from a murderer. The related inner-attitude and murder comparison preserves anger versus hatred and the different consequences.

Jesus describes laying down one’s life for friends as the greatest love. The letter identifies His laying down His life for us as known love and obliges laying down lives for brothers. The friends, us and brothers wording is retained without claiming identical groups.

James describes a brother or sister without clothing and food and rejects a farewell that supplies no bodily need. The letter tests love of God against possessing goods but closing one’s heart to a needy brother. Both give a concrete material-needs test of professed care.

James challenges warm words that give a needy person none of the body’s necessities. The letter commands love in deed and truth rather than word or tongue. The target supplies a specific example of speech without the corresponding act.

The preceding command places love in deed and truth rather than speech alone. The next by-this statement concerns knowing we are from the truth and reassuring the heart. The internal connection retains that concrete conduct-and-truth context without substituting an unrelated test.

Paul distinguishes his lack of awareness against himself from justification and leaves judgment to the Lord who discloses hidden things and hearts’ purposes. The letter places God’s greatness and all-knowingness above the condemning heart. The comparison preserves the different self-assessment statements without deciding every implication of God being greater.

Hebrews invites approaching the throne of grace with boldness for mercy and timely help. The letter links an uncondemning heart with confidence toward God. The related boldness/confidence descriptions preserve the distinct grounds rather than importing a new condition into Hebrews.

Jesus promises those remaining in Him, with His words remaining in them, that what they ask will be done. The letter connects receiving what is asked with keeping His commandments and pleasing Him. His words, rather than the disciples’ own words, are the stated condition in John; the remain and obedience formulations remain distinct.

Jesus describes God’s work as believing in the One He sent. The letter makes believing in the name of His Son Jesus Christ one part of His commandment. The target supports that believing clause without supplying the verse’s separate love-one-another command.

Jesus expressly commands love for one another as He loved the disciples. The letter joins loving one another with believing in His Son’s name in one commandment. This target supports the love clause, while the belief clause has a separate retained comparison.

Both connect knowledge of mutual abiding with the given Spirit. This verse also names keeping commandments; the later verse says He has given us of His Spirit. Those differences are preserved while the specific Spirit-and-abiding test is compared.

Paul joins not despising prophecies with testing everything and holding the good. The letter commands testing spirits because many false prophets have gone out. Both test prophetic claims rather than accepting every claim, with their different objects and instructions retained.

Second John describes deceivers not confessing Jesus Christ coming in flesh; this verse gives confessing Jesus Christ as having come in flesh as the test of a spirit from God. The coming and having-come forms remain distinct and are not replaced with a longer confession variant.

Both recall hearing that antichrist is coming and identify a present reality. Here the antichrist spirit is already in the world and does not confess Jesus; earlier many antichrists have arisen. The short does-not-confess-Jesus wording and plurality difference are preserved.

Jesus says He has overcome the world while addressing His disciples’ affliction. The letter says the children have overcome them because the One in them is greater than the one in the world. The different agents, objects and grounds of overcoming are retained.

Jesus says the world would love its own and hates those chosen out of it. The letter says those from the world speak from it and the world listens to them. Both describe affinity with the world and its corresponding reception, without equating every person or occasion.

Jesus connects being from God with hearing God’s words and explains His opponents’ failure to hear. The letter connects knowing God with listening to us and distinguishes truth from error. The shared hearing-and-belonging test preserves the different speakers and stated objects.

The earlier test identifies lack of brother-love with not being from God. This verse calls for mutual love and connects loving with birth from God and knowing Him. The positive and negative tests correspond without silently dropping the earlier righteousness criterion.

Both expressly say God is love. Here the absence of love exposes not knowing God; later abiding in love is joined to mutual abiding with God. The shared declaration supports the distinct negative and positive applications.

John connects God’s love for the world with giving the only-begotten Son and believers having eternal life. The letter describes God sending His only Son into the world so that we might live through Him. The only-begotten/only, giving/sending and life formulations remain distinct.

Romans describes God showing His love while we were sinners through Christ’s death for us. The letter locates love in God first loving us and sending His Son as propitiation. The target supplies a concrete prior divine act without substituting death wording for propitiation.

Jesus commands the disciples to love one another as He loved them. The letter reasons from God’s having loved us to our obligation to love one another. The prior-love and responsive-love pattern preserves the stated persons and formulations.

John says no one has ever seen God and names the only-begotten God at the Father’s bosom as making Him known. The letter says no one has beheld God and then speaks of mutual love and God abiding. Seen/beheld and the different following explanations remain distinct; John’s only-begotten God is not replaced with another variant.

Both identify the given Spirit as how mutual abiding is known. The earlier passage also names keeping His commandments; here He has given us of His Spirit. The specific abiding-and-Spirit correspondence preserves those different clauses.

The Samaritan hearers identify Jesus as Savior of the world after hearing for themselves. The letter bears witness that the Father sent the Son as Savior of the world. The shared title preserves the different witnesses and their stated grounds of testimony.

Romans joins confessing Jesus as Lord and believing God raised Him with salvation. The letter connects confessing Jesus as Son of God with mutual abiding. The confession content and promised consequence are related but not substituted as identical formulas.

Jesus calls disciples to remain in His love, relating His love to the Father’s and keeping commandments to remaining. The letter describes abiding in love as mutual abiding with God. The love-and-abiding connection preserves the different pronouns, conditions and declaration that God is love.

The earlier call to abide concerns confidence rather than shame at His manifestation and coming. This verse concerns completed love and confidence on the day of judgment. The shared confidence at an anticipated divine encounter preserves the differing grounds and descriptions.

Romans contrasts a spirit of slavery again toward fear with adoption and crying Abba, Father. The letter contrasts complete love with fear involving punishment. The fear and relational assurance comparison preserves slavery/adoption versus love/punishment rather than equating every use of fear.

The earlier statement says love begins not with our loving God but with His loving us and sending His Son. This verse expressly gives His first loving us as the ground of our love. The internal link retains the initiative-and-response order and the earlier sending clause.

The earlier test rejects being in light while hating a brother. This verse rejects claiming love for God while hating a brother as a lie and adds the seen/unseen argument. The same brother-hatred contradicts differently stated claims.

Jesus’s commandment expressly requires love for one another. The letter states that the person loving God must also love the brother. The concrete command to love fellow believers is shared, while the letter’s stated love-of-God premise remains its own clause.

John joins believing in His name with becoming children born of God rather than human bloods or will. The letter joins believing Jesus is the Christ with birth from God. The target supports the believing-and-birth clause without settling the further begetter/begotten love wording.

The earlier commandment joins believing in His Son’s name and loving one another. This verse tests love for God’s children by love for God and doing His commandments. The commandment-and-love correspondence preserves the different stated tests and the earlier explicit belief clause.

Jesus connects loving Him with keeping His commandments. The letter defines love of God through keeping His commandments and adds that they are not burdensome. The target supports love expressed through obedience without printing the additional burden claim.

Jesus declares that He has overcome the world. The letter states that everything born of God overcomes the world and names our faith as the victory. The shared overcoming preserves the different agent and the letter’s explicit faith and birth language.

The earlier verse says the children overcome them because the One in them is greater than the one in the world. Here overcoming the world is attributed to the one who believes that Jesus is God’s Son. The objects them/world and the stated grounds remain distinct.

John narrates blood and water flowing from Jesus’s pierced side and an eyewitness bearing true testimony. The letter describes Jesus coming through water and blood and the Spirit bearing witness as truth. The paired elements and testimony correspond without asserting that the letter defines them solely as that piercing event.

The next native verse supplies the three named witnesses introduced here: Spirit, water and blood, and their agreement. The short introductory unit is retained exactly; no heavenly-witness or expanded Comma wording is added to either verse.

The preceding two native units describe the Spirit as truth bearing witness and introduce three witnesses after mentioning water and blood. This verse names the Spirit, water and blood and their agreement. The retained explanatory context excludes this source unit itself and adds no expanded heavenly-witness text.

Jesus identifies the sending Father as bearing witness about Him. The letter says God’s testimony concerning His Son is greater than human testimony. The divine testimony about the Son corresponds, while the human/divine comparison is stated only in the letter.

Both passages describe making Him a liar. The earlier case denies having sinned; this case refuses God’s testimony concerning His Son. The uncommon accusation links specifically different rejected claims rather than identifying every case with the same offense.

Jesus says He gives His sheep eternal life. The letter testifies that God gave us eternal life and that this life is in His Son. The gift of eternal life corresponds while the giver, recipients and in-His-Son formulation remain as printed.

John connects believing in the Son with having eternal life and contrasts the person disobeying Him. The letter contrasts having the Son and life with not having the Son and life. Believing/disobeying and having/not-having are preserved as different formulations.

The Gospel states a purpose for written things involving belief that Jesus is Christ, God’s Son, and life in His name. The letter writes to name-believers so they may know they have eternal life. The purposes of belief and assurance are compared without treating the addressed readers as identical.

Jesus’s prayer submits the request about the cup to the Father’s will. The letter grounds confidence in being heard in asking according to His will. The specific prayer exemplifies submission to divine will without turning the letter into a promise of every requested outcome irrespective of that condition.

Jesus tells the disciples to ask the Father in His name and speaks of giving, receiving and full joy. The letter reasons from knowing He hears to knowing we have the requests. The Gospel’s name condition and the letter’s preceding will condition are retained rather than erased.

James connects prayer for a sick person with raising, conditional forgiveness and mutual prayer for healing. The letter directs asking for a brother sinning not toward death and distinguishes sin toward death. The related intercession preserves James’s sickness setting, conditional sins and the letter’s distinct death classification.

The earlier statement defines sin as lawlessness. This verse says all unrighteousness is sin and distinguishes sin not leading to death. The shared definition of wrongdoing preserves lawlessness versus unrighteousness and does not suppress the additional death qualification.

Both connect being born of God with not sinning. The earlier verse explains through abiding seed and inability to sin; this verse says the one born of God keeps himself and the evil one does not touch him. The keeps-himself wording and different explanations remain unaltered.

Jesus distinguishes those given His word from the world that hates them, saying they are not from the world, and asks that they be kept from the evil one. The letter contrasts being from God with the whole world lying in the evil one. The world/belonging and evil-one correspondence preserves the different groups and statements.

Jesus describes eternal life through knowing the only true God and Jesus Christ whom He sent. The letter connects the Son’s coming and understanding with knowing the True One and being in His Son Jesus Christ. The true-God and eternal-life language corresponds without deciding the letter’s final this antecedent beyond its wording.

Paul directs his beloved readers to flee idolatry. The letter tells little children to guard themselves from idols. The explicit prohibition concerns idolatrous objects and conduct without naming a particular idol or adding an unstated occasion.
